title: Shortages and price rises hit different households
oneline: Uzbekistan ran two energy-rationing regimes in three winters, and they burdened near-disjoint sets of households — the shortage hit the off-grid periphery, the price hit the connected core.

title: Who paid depended on gas connection, not income
oneline: Because the gas grid is urban, a universal energy subsidy was implicitly an urban/grid/big-user subsidy — so withdrawing it is governed by infrastructure access, not income.

title: Energy bills rose about 70%, almost all of it in winter
oneline: The 1 May 2024 tariff raised every household's energy bill ~70%, but the extra bite lands almost entirely in winter, on grid (piped-gas) households.

title: Annual averages hide the winter cost increase
oneline: The energy burden is a winter phenomenon that annual averages wash out completely.

title: Grid households fell behind on winter bills after the reform
oneline: Post-reform, grid households face an extra winter payment-distress bite that the annual average hides.

title: Electricity supply improved before the tariff, not because of it
oneline: Winter 2024/25 was the most reliable winter in the panel and the most financially distressed — but the reliability recovery began a year earlier, when Russian gas imports started, before the tariff.

title: Payment problems spiked twice, for two different reasons
oneline: Grid-household payment distress spikes exactly twice — the 2022/23 supply crisis and the 2024/25 price winter — with a clean zero in between.

title: Farm income gains were measurable, energy losses were not
oneline: Estimating both arms in one model, the gains (ag income, better economic sentiment) show up cleanly at the household level while the losses don't appear as welfare damage — the aggregation-bias argument made structural.

title: Inflation stayed flat in 2024 while every neighbour's fell
oneline: The repricing is invisible in headline inflation because the tariff shock absorbed a global disinflation that every regional peer enjoyed in 2024.

title: Energy use barely changed after prices rose
oneline: The reform's stated goal was conservation; physical energy use barely moved, so it was a pure income transfer, not an efficiency gain.

title: Compensation for the tariff reached 16 households
oneline: The income-targeted compensation for the tariff failed structurally — it reached almost no one — because the losers are defined by grid access, not income.

title: An 1888 railway still predicts local wealth
oneline: The 1888–1906 Trans-Caspian railway still predicts local wealth 130 years later.

title: Gas-producing regions have the least gas access
oneline: The gas-producing regions have the lowest domestic gas access — grid access reflects Soviet political-distribution choices, not geology or income.

title: Uzbekistan stopped being a gas exporter
oneline: The rent that paid for cheap gas evaporated exactly as households were asked to pay more — this is the "why now."

title: Cotton prices fell while almost every other crop rose
oneline: The 2024 ag package looks like industrial policy (clusters, per-ha subsidy, export promotion) but behaves like rent-recomposition — transfers, not productive transformation.

title: Claims that did not survive further testing
oneline: The honesty ledger — things that looked true in a naive comparison but did not survive household fixed effects, and the claims we therefore dropped.

title: Approaches that were tried and abandoned
oneline: Two systematic hunts for an alternative identification strategy.

title: Vocational enrolment collapsed after the 2017 reform
oneline: Uzbekistan's 1997 compulsory-vocational reform and its 2017 reversal produce one of the sharpest cohort discontinuities in survey data — possibly the only modern case of a state removing compulsory schooling years — but the outcome window hasn't matured.

title: Other findings from the wider data
oneline: A reservoir of facts from the wide all-data exploration.
